Hydrants Show Off

Their Personalities

Photographers usually see things through different eyes than most people. It’s a condition of

Over the years as photgrapher William E. John made his rounds looking for interesting shots, he became aware of fire hydrants.

“I began to notice that fire hydrants were dif- ferent, that each one had its own personality. That’s how I started taking pictures of them.”

And that’s how this series was born. John hunkered. down and focussed his camera on the hydrants, catching them on film in ways that seemed to give them an almost-human aspect.

Democracy Roams B.C. Woods

By DON COLLINS Colonist Labor Reporter

One day soon stacks of pamphlets will find their way into the hands of millworkers and many of the others who toil for their living in the forest industry of B.C.

It will be part of the bienni- al pitch to the rank-and-file members of the International from the men who would like Woodworkers of America to influence the western Cana- da leadership vote.

There will also be the cus- tomary visits from those seek- ing office and those beating the drums on their behalf.

You might call it politics served up IWA-style.

It is a very natural thing with -an organization that is the biggest industrial union in the West (42,000 members) and which likes to look on it- self as the most-democratic.

Most unions today allow convention delegates to elect their top officers. The IWA permits nominations only at its conventions and takes the actual vote to the mem- bership at large.

All in the name of democra- Cyn

‘The union says it is tightly controlled this way by the rank-and-file. And so far the same rank-and-file hasn't pro- posed a better way to run things.

Generally- this makes for noisy political’ conventions, but the IWA western regional convention that wound up last Friday at Vancouver was unu- sually quiet.

Student Election Method Rapped

University of Victoria sen- ate: at a meeting Wednesday tabled a motion criticizing methods being used hy the Alma Mater Society in elect- ing student representatives to the university academic go- verning body.

Student, senator Derry McDonell said the student council and the student news- paper, the Martlet, had re- fused to publicize the names of those seeking election to the senate.

McDonell told the senate. he had asked -that the student body postpone the election, set for this Friday, for one week to enable students to learn who was running and what the candidate's plat- forms comprised. He said his request-had been refused.

He reminded senate that ir- regularities in student voting procedures last year resulted in a month-long delay in seat-

ing stiident representatives on senate.

David Dunsmuir, represent- ing. graduate students, said he, ‘was yery much disap- pointed in the manner. in which the Alma Mater Society is conducting-its election but I believe they should be left to make a botch of it in their own way. But this is a very bad thing on the face of it.”

After hearing an appeal by McDonell that the senate ‘de- plore the insulting and infan- tile behavior of. the student executive council’ it was de- ¢ided to table the motion.

So far there has been no publicity on campus about the election and no opportunity has been afforded student candidates to make their views public in the student

“nominations for all student positions closed last Friday, the’ day after we published.”

‘These are the presidents of some of the big, influential coast locals and while they have been dubbed members of the presidents’ club, they deny any such organized enemy camp ever existed.

Opposition to what they see as the ineffective leadership of the 48-year-old Moore is written off by them as grassroots opposition.

One of their members, Mur- ray Drew, who heads the 2,100-member Victoria local, says this was the real reason on the last day of the conven- tion for rejection of a pro- posed salary increase for the leaders.

A close standing vote meant Moore and his regional of- ficers wouldn't get their raise after all and it was seen as a telling blow scored by the op- position.

“This is really a sign of the dissatisfaction of the rank- and-file,” Drew said in an in- terview Wednesday. “I think it shows that the membership of the locals is not prepared to support the leaders.”

Drew, of course, is wielding a political axe.

When the time comes to carry the election message to the members of his logal, he says his officers “certainly won’t be supporting the ad- ministration.”

Syd Thompson, whose 7,000- member Vancouver local is the biggest of all, fully ex- pects his men will sound the call for an anti-administration vote. But that will have to wait until his executive meets Friday and the membership meets Saturday.

‘These are some of the obvi- ous signs of the Bolitics within the IWA. There are. others

that don’t come up in conven- tion business.

Another touch of politics in- volves the attempt by the re- gional officers to dump one of their own men, _secretary- treasurer Fred Fieber, in favor of replacing him with an old enemy — Duncan local president Weldon Jubenville.

“Jubie,” long” associated with Drew, Thompson, log- gers local president Ernie Freer and New Westminster local president Gerr Stoney, successfully switched camps last spring when he served as secretary of the coast nego- tiating committee.

Lost Expedition.

Environment Minister Jack Davis dodged pro- testing Indian fishermen all day Wednesday in Port Alberni before firt ally meeting with them to discuss native fishing rights.

Davis met with the Indians in Port Alberni’s Indian Friendship Centre at about 6. p.m. He listened to chiefs re- presenting 10 bands and pro- mised that today (Thursday) he would send a federal fis eries representative to Tofino to assess the sockeye salmon situation to see if there are enough of the sockeye to let the Indians fish.

Earlier Wednesday, Davis avoided a public confrontation with about 100 persons repre- senting bands from the Port Alberni and Tofino areas.

The Indians were protesting for the second time since Monday a commercial fishing ban on sockeye salmon in To- fino Inlet. They claim the clo- sure prohibits them from tak- ing fish for food. A group of Indians — about 200 — dem- onstrated peacefully Monday against the ban outside the federal building at Tofino.

Davis toured the Port Al- berni harbor Wednesday and Indian demonstrators were waiting at the dock to meet him, But Davis landed at an- other point and went immédi- ately to a private meeting with Port Alberni commercial fishermen.

He had agreed earlier to a private meeting with the protesting Indians.

Mrs. Barney Williams of Tofino, whose husband, or- ganized the protest, said the group is “happy that he's doing something, anyway.”

Indians have been granted permits each fall to spear, gaff or net salmon, rather than fish for them in conven- tional manner.

Main point at issue is that the Indians regard their fish- ing habits as native right and not, as Chief Simon Lucas of the Hesquihat band says; “some kind of privilege hand- ed out by white men working for the government.”
